Birdman

By: Liz Fish | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
He flys through the air at 400km an hour, just using gravity and the air under his wingsuit- he's the second fastest person in the world- for now

Unique Selling Point:
As children we have all dreamt of being able to fly like a bird, and I still have dreams where I am flying, wingsuit flying is truly the embodiment of the dream of human flight, and South African Jean Jacques Wallis has just proved he is the 2nd fastest person in the world, the fastest person was just 6 hundredths of a second faster. On the 16th September competing against the top 16 fastest pilots in the world at the 10th Wingsuit Grand Prix in China JJ flew at speeds of over 230 km per hour, completing the 4000 meter course in 24,766 seconds, just +0,063 slower than the fastest – Australian Tahi Munroe 24,703 – less than a blink of an eye. The type of gaps you see in F1 racing.

Summary:
The WWL is a huge event, sponsored by the Chinese Government launching off the majestic Tianmen Mountain. The 10th World Wingsuit League Competition has just taken place in the Hunan Province, China. Its, the world’s most daring air sports competition. The pilot’s flying performance is truly incredible when you consider they only have gravity as their engine.
Free fall flight has many different disciplines, and the Grand Prix includes two- speed flying and target accuracy competition. Each of the pilots strikes a paper target in flight, much like human archery. The pilots wear a pole on their helmets to pierce the target and a high-speed camera is used to judge the score. The target is a 1m square, piece of paper and they launch at 1 kilometre away and the pilots are travelling at over 180km/h! All 3 winners scored a bullseye- just 10 cm wide - in the final round and so they had to look back at the practice rounds to see who won.
JJ grew up skydiving and by the time he was 12 he had done his 1st tandem dive. By Grade 8 he completed his accelerated freefall course, and by 18 he had completed over 1000 jumps. At 35 he has done 14 000 jumps and many 1000 base jumps and miraculously has never been injured. He describes it as like being in a giant swimming pool and moving through it like a fish and the more he fly’s the more he unlocks a matrix of moves. He is way past being an adrenalin junkie- he is perfecting his ability to fly.
The sport of wingsuit flying takes skydiving and BASE (Building, Antenna, Span, and Earth) jumping to a new level. Skydivers and BASE jumpers jump out of planes or off tall objects, free fall, and pull a parachute before they get too close to the ground. Wingsuit flyers, on the other hand, wear suits that allow them to glide through the air before they eventually lose altitude and pull their parachutes. The flying squirrel-like suits are made of highly durable fabric and have two wings, one below the arms and one between the legs, creating a flat surface to make gliding possible. As the flyer shoots forward, small adjustments to their body position drastically affect their trajectory. This makes steering intuitive, at the WWL they did a circuit where they were not allowed 7meter from various obstacles flying at speeds of over 200km.
The art of wingsuit flying is 120 years old, 96% of the flyers have died testing these suits but the more scientists apply their minds to this desperate craving to fly, the safer the suits are getting.
JJ most regular jump is off Table Mountain, he spends about R30 000 a year on the cable car. When he started there were just 3 jumps- now he has developed over 50. 80 seconds of freefall and 30 seconds in the parachute- crazy fast.


Further information:
JJ is an extreme athlete, in school he got distinctions for maths and geography , flying is not a matter of jumping off a cliff and taking your chances, it filled with calculations, wind speeds and air density. Its should be an Olympic sport- in fact Olympic judges adjudicate the big competitions.

Extra Budget Items:
Tandem Skydiving jump is R4000 which we hope the presenter will do. WE will also need to stay over in Wellington close to the drop zone and the Bains Kloof where we will do the base jumps so we can start early. The presenter will need to fly in the night before as we start climbing at 1st light to the Base jump- beautiful pictures

JJ “The feeling of flying feels like floating in dry water.

pure, pure, blissfulness and, serenity.. Nothing else matters. Nothing else is in your mind. You're just thinking about your flight. Where are you going
VO: Perfecting the art of flying – dreams from childhood - pursued for centuries.
This is the purest form of human flight - and Jean Jacques Wallis is one of the best in the world
VO: He’s just returned from China, where he became the world’s second-fastest wingsuiter, hitting an astonishing top speed of 230 kilometres an hour.
Breather
VO: Often seen as the realm of reckless daredevils with a death wish, the history of free flight certainly includes many tragic accidents. However, it has evolved into a highly skilled and respected professional sport.
Upsound JJ looking at the weather
VO: We are spending a couple of days getting to know JJ, and we’re accompanying him as he attempts a world first.
JJ “One step in front of the other”
VO: Described as half mountain goat, half eagle by friends, JJ sees these mountains in the Du Toits Kloof outside Paarl as potential for new jumps with a lifetime of adventure ahead. Today, his wife Katie is joining us.
Govan “ You know I have massively underestimated how unfit I am
JJ“, we have got a whole mountain ahead of us here, so here we go, one step in front of each other
VO: JJ had convinced us it was a short hike - but at 38 degrees we were suffering
JJ: It is going to take maybe another 30 to 40 minutes, The wind is looking great,
Govan “The way you describing this hike it's so casual but its not Bro”
JJ” It's the most casual one that's 7 hours of hiking, that's 4 hours, they all better jumps- lets go do the little jump
Govan “Lets just go”
Govan Link” It's not just about just jumping off the side of the mountain it's about getting here and I can tell you right now you need to be an athlete to finish this hike, I don't know how I am going to get down, but JJ comes here all the time.”
VO: You might be wondering how any of this makes sense and what it takes to get to this point
JJ: I got introduced to skydiving at a young age, and I think it made me aware of what is possible in life. And the sky's is a playground and you can fly in it and abuse it.
VO: At just 3, JJ was watching parachutes being packed at his uncle’s skydiving company. The sport was in his family, and so at 16 he had his accredited freefall licence, and by 18 he was skydiving full time
JJ: Flying. I think it's very artistic to fly. Has a lot of, uh, creativity. And you can express yourself in the mountains. You can draw lines down the mountain wherever you want to.
Govan: What kind of speeds are we talking about?
JJ: in the performance competitions in the skydiving world, we're seeing up to 400 K per hour
VO: The day before this epic trek, I’d seen the planning that goes into these jumps. Nothing is left to chance.
JJ: it's a very high performance wingsuit.. Our feet basically control the turning left and right
Govan: Anything special about the helmet?
JJ: No, …We put the GPS on the back of the helmet, and then when we jump afterwards on the computers, we're able to analyse the data
Link: Wingsuit base jumping is incredibly dangerous, but being in this room you get a sense of how much the sport has developed over the last two decades
JJ “Ja you can see the flight in full 3D
VO: Advances in weather mapping and GPS data recording has made the sport very technical
JJ “ And this is a jump I did at the tunnel. And, The Huguenot tunnel -And on this flight, you can see I flew, uh, a total of 48 seconds in the freefall, and I did 22 seconds under the parachute.
Govan: Does it help you make it safer?
JJ: Yeah, it makes it much safer because then you're not jumping blind. You're not going into the unknown.
VO: As one of the top 16 wingsuit pilots in the world - he competed in the 10th World Wingsuit league hosted by China in September.
Dropping off the Yuhu Peak on the Tianmen Mountain in just 24,766 seconds, he became the world’s 2nd fastest wingsuiter. He missed 1st place by 6 hundredths of a second.
JJ: The one is a speed race down the mountain in the Slalem course. And then we compete in a target competition. And that's basically where we have a stick on our helmet and right next to the spectators there is a piece of paper with the bull's eye, about the size of an Oreo.
VO: Launching from one kilometer away JJ also took 2nd place in the target competition
VO: Back to his day job as a tandem instructor. This is how JJ perfects his skills- and pays the bills. With 14 000 jumps under his wings he has had a lot of practice
Link “So this is where skydivers hang out, it’s called a drop zone, it’s the heart of the community, they share information here, they plan their jumps and they do postmortems, it a really important part of this sport and the industry
VO: The drop zone is also where he met his wife Katie- who surprisingly - isn’t a skydiver
Katie:I like going fast in cars. I like driving cars. I always have, like, this joke with him. Like, he's a really good pilot in, like, flying things. Yeah, but he's a really bad driver. He really is.
VO: JJ never attempts a new jump without consulting her first.
Govan: as much as it's exciting it's dangerous right.
Katie: That's why you go through all the training and the more experienced you are, the more, um, knowledge you gain and the more you hang out with more experienced people, the more experience and knowledge you gain from them too.
VO: If I really wanted to understand JJ’s passion for flight - I needed to get a taste of it myself
JJ “It takes about 10 minutes to go up in the aeroplane
How you feeling - Govan I am feeling alright,
LINK in the air; “This entire time I didn’t really realise what JJ was talking about but this is it, the feeling of flying and I can see why he loves this sport so much
VO: Back in the Du Toits Kloof - it took 4 hours to get to the cliffs above the Huguenot tunnel to a jump he’s called Tunnel vision, and fortunately the conditions were perfect.
Govan: Are you scared when you jump?
JJ: Scared? I would say if you're not scared of dying, there's something wrong. But I think most people are scared, are not living enough in their lives. So that's what all skydivers and base jumpers are trying to do. We're just trying to, like, suck the marrow out of life and do what we can.
Govan: I am sweating and I am not even jumping bro,
JJ “I am so stoke you here, see you on the bottom ,
“ Love you, love you lots
GOVAN “Oh my god he is flying he is flying for real.
VO: That is a world first, JJ flew under the Du Toit’s Kloof bridge at 227 km an hour
Govan” that is incredible,
VO: It's said when once you have tasted flight, you will forever walk the earth with your eyes turned to the sky.

At 35 he has done 14 000 jumps and many 1000 base jumps and miraculously has never been injured. He describes it as like being in a giant swimming pool and moving through it like a fish and the more he fly’s the more he unlocks a matrix of moves. He is way past being an adrenalin junkie- he is perfecting his ability to fly. The sport of wingsuit flying takes skydiving and BASE (Building, Antenna, Span, and Earth) jumping to a new level. Skydivers and BASE jumpers jump out of planes or off tall objects, free fall, and pull a parachute before they get too close to the ground. Wingsuit flyers, on the other hand, wear suits that allow them to glide through the air before they eventually lose altitude and pull their parachutes. The flying squirrel-like suits are made of highly durable fabric and have two wings, one below the arms and one between the legs, creating a flat surface to make gliding possible. As the flyer shoots forward, small adjustments to their body position drastically affect their trajectory. This makes steering intuitive, at the WWL they did a circuit where they were not allowed 7meter from various obstacles flying at speeds of over 200km. The art of wingsuit flying is 120 years old, 96% of the flyers have died testing these suits but the more scientists apply their minds to this desperate craving to fly, the safer the suits are getting. JJ most regular jump is off Table Mountain, he spends about R30 000 a year on the cable car. When he started there were just 3 jumps- now he has developed over 50. 80 seconds of freefall and 30 seconds in the parachute- crazy fast.
metadata.Further information: JJ is an extreme athlete, in school he got distinctions for maths and geography , flying is not a matter of jumping off a cliff and taking your chances, it filled with calculations, wind speeds and air density. Its should be an Olympic sport- in fact Olympic judges adjudicate the big competitions.
